definition.text: A regressive tax is one whose rate falls as the amount being taxed rises, so poorer people pay a larger share of what they have.

facts.text: A tax can also count as regressive when the taxed activity is done more by the poor than by the rich.
Its opposite, a progressive tax, takes a higher percentage from those with higher incomes.
Taxes on everyday essentials such as food, fuel, energy and housing, including carbon taxes, are often regressive.
Because spending on necessities like food barely rises with income, such taxes weigh most heavily on lower-income households.
Some governments give rebates to lower-income households to soften the effect.
A number of studies find a carbon tax without extra benefits or tax credits hits poor households harder than rich ones.

definition.text: Road pricing means charging drivers directly for road use, through tolls, distance or time fees, congestion charges or charges on more polluting vehicles.

facts.text: The charges may mainly raise money for roads or manage demand to cut congestion, pollution, noise and crashes.
William Vickrey built on Pigou's ideas to make the theoretical case for road pricing in the 1950s, proposing electronic charging for busy roads.
Distance-based lorry charges in Austria (2004) and Germany (2005) vary by emissions level and axles.
A Stockholm study found that without congestion pricing the city's air would have been five to ten percent more polluted in 2006–2010, with 45 percent more asthma attacks in young children.

conflicts.text: The Congestion pricing article reports the same Stockholm finding as 5 to 15 percent more polluted air.
conflicts.note: Two articles quote the same Stockholm 2006–2010 study with different upper bounds.

definition.text: A sin tax is an excise on goods and services seen as harmful, such as alcohol, tobacco, sugar, gambling or polluting vehicles.

facts.text: Unlike a Pigouvian tax, which charges for the damage done to others, a sin tax raises the price mainly to cut use.
Raising a sin tax is often more popular than raising other taxes.
Critics call sin taxes regressive and say they encourage smuggling and black markets.
A government may come to depend on the revenue and so need the 'sinful' behaviour to continue.
